title: Door-in-the-Face
description: Asking for something absolutely huge and unreasonable, getting rejected, then compromising.

sections.title: Quick Understanding
sections.content: Asking for something absolutely huge and unreasonable, getting predictably rejected, then immediately 'compromising' with a much smaller request (which was your real goal all along).

sections.title: Why It Works
sections.content: Reciprocal concession. If you make a massive concession (dropping your huge request down to a small one), the social rules of reciprocity dictate that the other person must also make a concession (dropping their 'no' down to a 'yes').

sections.title: Real-Life Examples
content: Daily Life: 'Can I borrow $1000?' -> 'No.' -> 'Okay, can I just borrow $50?'
Sales: Pitching the extreme $50,000 package first, then dropping generously to the $5,000 package.
Workplace: Asking your boss for 4 weeks of vacation, settling happily for the 2 weeks you actually wanted.
Kids: 'Mom, can I get a massive pony?' -> 'No.' -> 'Can I get a hamster?'

sections.title: What It Looks Like
content: Charity Caller: 'Would you be willing to donate $500 to our historical fund today?'
You: 'Absolutely not, I can't afford that.'
Charity Caller: 'I completely understand that is a lot. Would you consider just a $20 donation instead just to help out?'
You: (Relieved) 'Oh, well... yeah, I can do $20.'

sections.title: Pattern Recognition
content: An initial request that is ridiculously, insultingly high.
An immediate, pre-planned pivot to a smaller request the precise second you say no.
The second request suddenly seeming very reasonable purely by contrast.

sections.title: Ethical Uses
sections.content: Starting negotiations high to find the true market value, while being completely willing to physically compromise fairly.

sections.title: Manipulative Uses
sections.content: Intentionally terrifying a buyer with an impossible price purely to manufacture guilt and manipulate them into taking a terrible 'compromise' deal they otherwise would have rejected.

sections.title: Red Flags
content: The first request is so high it is almost comical.
The person doesn't even attempt to argue when you say no; they just instantly drop the price.
The 'compromise' happens within 2 seconds of the total rejection.

sections.title: Defense Strategies
content: Judge the second request entirely independently. Ask: 'Would I say yes to this if it was the very first thing they asked me?'
Call out the tactic explicitly: 'Are you just anchoring me extremely high so I agree to the smaller one?'
Make your own counter-offer instead of blindly accepting their 'concession'.

sections.title: Mistakes People Make
content: Feeling immensely, physically relieved by the smaller request and saying yes purely out of gratitude.
Feeling socially obligated to 'meet them in the middle' simply because they dropped their arbitrary price.

sections.title: Case Study
sections.content: Researchers asked college students to volunteer to chaperone juvenile delinquents on a zoo trip. Only 17% agreed. For a second group, researchers first asked if the students would explicitly commit to volunteering 2 hours a week for 2 solid years as counselors. 100% refused. Immediately after the refusal, the researcher asked, 'Well, would you at least chaperone a simple one-time zoo trip?' Agreement massively shot up to 50%.

sections.title: Key Lessons
content: 1. Extreme rejection is part of the plan.
2. The second request is the only real request.
3. Do not feel obligated to compromise back.
4. Judge the second request in a total vacuum.
